meta.title: Prelude No. 1 in C major, BWV 846

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Johann Sebastian Bach, Prelude No. 1 in C major, BWV 846, from The Well-Tempered Clavier, Book I (compiled by 1722, public domain; Bach died 1750). 35 measures, consisting almost entirely of a one-bar broken-chord figure (an eighth rest plus six 16th notes, played twice per bar) over a sustained bass note and a tied inner voice, with a written-out flourish replacing the repeat in the final three bars.

meta.subtitle: from The Well-Tempered Clavier, Book I
meta.trains: Continuous right-hand arpeggiation over a sustained left-hand bass and an inner tied suspension voice; harmonic listening bar-to-bar (each measure is one implied chord); evenness of tone as the hand shifts position across 35 measures without a rest longer than an eighth note.

meta.title: l'Arabesque (25 Etudes faciles, Op. 100, No. 2)

provenance.credit: Typeset by Bas Wassink for the Mutopia Project

meta.subtitle: Arabeske
meta.trains: Quick 16th-note turn figures answered by a light eighth-note tag, alternating with a lyrical dotted-quarter melody, over a steady broken-chord left hand in A minor - finger agility and voicing a short melodic cell cleanly at a scherzando tempo.

meta.title: Prelude in C minor, Op. 28 No. 20
meta.subtitle: "Funeral March"
meta.trains: Dense, widely-spread four- and five-note block chords in both hands (up to a minor 10th), a full ff-to-pp dynamic range with two written crescendi, and a two-layer right-hand texture (a sustained chord against a decorative turn figure) that asks for careful voicing and pedalling rather than finger speed.
limitations: Written pedal is not played by the engine (facts.hasPedal is informational only).

Slurs and the exact hairpin start/stop beat positions from the source engraving are approximated, not reproduced to the exact beat; they do not change the sounding pitches, rhythm or overall dynamic shape.

meta.title: Prelude in E minor, Op. 28 No. 4 ("Largo")
meta.subtitle: Arrangement (playable hand-span fixes)
meta.trains: Chromatic voice leading, sustained dissonance, a wide dynamic range, and rhythmic independence between a slow-moving right-hand line and pulsing left-hand chords.
limitations: Pedal is not written or played; performers commonly sustain this prelude with continuous pedal, which this file does not encode.
departures: Measure 10 (bar 9): changed left-hand suspended B4 to B3 to fit hand-span cap.
Measure 24 (bar 23): changed left-hand bass octave B1 to B2 to fit hand-span cap.

meta.title: Sonatina in C major, Op. 36 No. 1 (1st movement, exposition)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Muzio Clementi, Sonatina in C major, Op. 36 No. 1 (published 1797, public domain; Clementi died 1832), 1st movement (Spiritoso). Pitches and rhythm for measures 1-15 (both hands) were transcribed and checked note-by-note against the Mutopia Project's public-domain LilyPond engraving (piece-info id 804, sonatina-1.ly, after the G. Schirmer 1893 Sonatina Album edition), including cross-checking the relative-octave arithmetic against the piece's well-known melodic contour and against the internal harmonic/voice-leading consistency of the reconstructed left hand.
provenance.note: Exposition only (the source's own measures 1-15, up to its written repeat sign), played once; the notated repeat back to measure 1, and the movement's development/recapitulation (measures 16-38 of the source), are not included. The 'Spiritoso' marking is Clementi's, but the metronome mark is the Schirmer editor's; it was lowered from 156 to 144 for this file so it sits inside this level's tempo cap while keeping the 'Spiritoso' character.

meta.subtitle: Spiritoso - exposition only, repeat not taken
meta.trains: A brisk single-line melody in the right hand (scale runs, octave leaps, a brief secondary-dominant tonicization) over a light, mostly on-the-beat left hand - reading fluency and a fast, even tempo more than technical difficulty.
limitations: tempo lowered to 144 to fit level (source's 156 is editorial)

meta.title: Für Elise, WoO 59

provenance.credit: Typeset by Stelios Samelis for the Mutopia Project (Mutopia-2015/08/18-931) from the Breitkopf & Härtel edition of 1888, and placed in the public domain by the typesetter.
provenance.note: Converted from Mutopia's LilyPond source to MusicXML (notes, rests, repeats and voltas, grace notes, triplets, 8va, clefs, slurs, dynamics, pedal); beams and accidentals then completed by pnpm library:engrave. Checked mechanically: all 902 non-grace notes match Mutopia's own MIDI file in pitch and written onset, and the three grace notes are the only notes the MIDI has in addition. 106 measures, as in Mutopia's engraving.

meta.subtitle: Complete piece, from the Breitkopf & Härtel edition (1888) via the Mutopia Project
meta.trains: The whole rondo as Beethoven wrote it: the A theme over broken-chord bass, the F-major episode with its grace notes and 32nd-note figures, the agitated C section over a repeated bass pedal, and the triplet arpeggio run up under an 8va and back down chromatically.
limitations: The first-ending bar and the final bar are two eighths long (together with the pickup they make a full bar, as printed), so opening the piece shows an information notice about measure length.

meta.title: Gymnopedie No. 1

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Satie, Trois Gymnopedies, No. 1 (public domain, composed 1888). Key (2 sharps), tempo marking (Lent et douloureux, quarter = 50), metre (3/4), the alternating low-bass/high-chord left-hand accompaniment pattern and the right-hand melody's entrance in measure 5 were checked against the Mutopia Project's public-domain LilyPond edition (piece-info id 37, gymnopedie_1, typeset by Evin Robertson from the Dover Edition).
provenance.note: The left-hand voicing - a low bass note answered by a chord roughly two octaves higher - is authentic to the source, not a simplification; it is why this piece computes to Advanced (criteria 16 and 17) rather than the Intermediate shelf it was first drafted for.

meta.subtitle: cross-checked against the Mutopia Project edition
meta.trains: A wide-spanning left hand alternating a low bass note with a chord high above it (up to a two-and-a-half-octave leap), sustained pedal colour, ties held across barlines and soft, patient dynamic shading (pp/p/mp/f) at a slow tempo.

meta.title: Amazing Grace (arranged for beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: The hymn tune "New Britain" (the "Amazing Grace" tune; Virginia Harmony, 1831) in the form harmonized by E. O. Excell (1900), both public domain. The melody is the Soprano of the Mutopia Project's public-domain LilyPond engraving (piece-info id 1283, new_britain.ly, typeset by Steve Dunlop from www.cyberhymnal.org); the audit record content/library/audit/repertoire/beginner/amazing-grace.json re-checks it note by note.
provenance.note: A one-beat pickup and 15 bars in G major at quarter = 72. The right hand plays the tune exactly as the source gives it, rhythm included; the left hand holds one bass note per bar.

meta.subtitle: Hymn tune "New Britain", simple two-hand setting in 3/4
meta.trains: A well-known pentatonic melody with a one-beat pickup, in half, quarter and a few eighth notes, over a single sustained bass note per bar - gentle two-hand reading at a slow tempo.
departures: Left hand: our own single held bass note per bar, taken from the bass of E. O. Excell's harmonization, instead of his four-part harmony.

meta.title: Fur Elise (opening motif, arranged for absolute beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Beethoven, Fur Elise, WoO 59 (public domain, composed c. 1810), opening only. The quoted bars were checked against the Mutopia Project's public-domain LilyPond engraving (piece-info id 931, fur_Elise_WoO59.ly, typeset by Stelios Samelis from the Breitkopf & Härtel edition of 1888); the audit record content/library/audit/repertoire/beginner/fur-elise-theme-16-bar.json re-runs that check.
provenance.note: A different, much simpler arrangement from the intermediate Fur Elise item. The pickup and bars 1-4 follow Beethoven's melody with every value doubled (3/8 written as 3/4), with the changes listed in departures; bars 5-16 are our own. The left hand is a single sustained bass note per bar and rests under the opening figure, as in Beethoven's own texture there. 17 written measures (a one-beat pickup plus 16 bars) at quarter = 60.

meta.subtitle: 16-bar beginner arrangement: melody with a single bass note per bar
meta.trains: The famous opening motif read at a gentle tempo with eighth notes at most, over a single left-hand bass note per bar - the hands barely need to coordinate.
departures: Metre and values: Beethoven's 3/8 is written as 3/4 with every note value doubled (sixteenths become eighths).
Bar 1: the third E is a quarter note and the C that leads to bar 2's A is left out (Beethoven: E-D#-E-B-D-C in even notes), so no more than four equal notes follow each other.
Bars 3-4: no accidentals after bar 1 - G instead of G-sharp in bar 3, D instead of D-sharp at the end of bar 4.
Bars 5-16 are our own continuation in A minor, not Beethoven's; bars 9-12 and 13-16 repeat bars 5-8.
Left hand: our own single bass note per bar (A or E) instead of Beethoven's broken chords.

meta.title: Greensleeves (arranged for beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Traditional English ballad melody "Greensleeves" (16th century; public domain, author unknown). The tune's traditional metre is 6/8; we re-set it in 3/4 here as a beginner simplification, following the same practice used by several published easy-piano editions of this tune (e.g. 8notes.com's "Greensleeves (beginners)", music-for-music-teachers.com's 3/4 arrangement, lasolsheet.com's beginner edition). The melody's overall shape and the block left-hand bass roots (one sustained note per bar, natural A-minor throughout, no raised leading tone) are our own simple two-hand setting, not a transcription of any specific published edition.
provenance.note: 16-bar folk-song form (four 4-bar phrases) with a one-beat pickup, ending on the A-minor tonic. Left hand plays exactly one sustained bass note per measure, so the hands are never independently active in the same bar (hand-independence fraction 0).

meta.subtitle: Traditional English melody, simple two-hand setting in 3/4
meta.trains: A well-known, mostly stepwise melody over a single sustained bass note per bar - reading two staves together at a gentle tempo.

meta.title: Jingle Bells (opening refrain, arranged for beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: James Lord Pierpont's song, copyrighted September 16, 1857 as "The One Horse Open Sleigh" and reissued in 1859 as "Jingle Bells" (public domain in the United States as a pre-1928 publication). Verified via Boston University's "History of Jingle Bells" article and the song's Wikipedia entry, both confirming the 1857 copyright, Pierpont's authorship and the original title.
provenance.note: Only the familiar opening refrain ("Jingle bells, jingle bells, jingle all the way / Oh what fun it is to ride in a one-horse open sleigh") is arranged here, 8 bars, key of C major, quarter=96 - not the full song with its verses. The original's faster note groupings on "ride in a one-horse" are simplified to plain quarter notes so the shortest value stays inside the Beginner cap; the melodic contour otherwise follows the well-known tune. The left-hand single bass note per bar is our own simple setting; arrangement is reflected in the title per FR-007.

meta.subtitle: "Jingle bells, jingle bells, jingle all the way" - simple two-hand setting
meta.trains: A very well-known, mostly repeated-note and stepwise melody in quarter/half notes over a single sustained bass note per bar, at a brisk tempo.

meta.title: Mary Had a Little Lamb (arranged for beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Sarah Josepha Hale's poem "Mary's Lamb" was published in Boston in 1830 (public domain). The now-familiar melody is generally traced to the mid-19th-century minstrel tune "Goodnight, Ladies" rather than to any 1830 setting, and is of traditional/uncertain authorship - both the poem and the tune are long in the public domain. Verified via the Classical Music (classical-music.com) history article and Wikipedia's Sarah Josepha Hale entry, which agree on the 1830 poem date and the tune's later, separate, traditional origin.
provenance.note: 8-bar beginner form transposed to F major so the melody sits in a single five-finger hand position (F-G-A-Bb-C), quarter=96. The left-hand single bass note per bar (I-V) is our own simple setting; the published original has no piano accompaniment of its own.

meta.subtitle: Traditional American melody, five-finger setting in F major
meta.trains: A very well-known three/four-note melody that never leaves a five-finger hand position, over a single sustained bass note per bar - an easy first piece for a fixed hand position.

meta.title: Ode to Joy (theme, arranged for beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Beethoven, "Ode to Joy" theme (Symphony No. 9, 4th movement; public domain, traditional beginner melody). The left-hand I-IV-V-I block-chord accompaniment is our own simple setting.
provenance.note: The first two 4-bar phrases only, ending on the tonic; not the complete symphonic theme.

meta.subtitle: Theme from Symphony No. 9, simple two-hand arrangement
meta.trains: A simple stepwise melody with steady quarter notes over static left-hand chords - an easy introduction to playing both hands together.

meta.title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star (arranged for beginners)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: The tune "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" is the French folk melody "Ah! vous dirai-je, Maman", first published c. 1761 from an earlier c. 1740 tune (public domain); the English nursery-rhyme text is Jane Taylor's 1806 poem, also public domain. The melody is the same one Mozart used, decades later, as the theme for his Twelve Variations K. 265 - the tune itself long predates and is independent of that set. Verified via the tune's Wikipedia history entry and the Wikipedia entry for Mozart's K. 265 variations.
provenance.note: Standard 12-bar AABA beginner form (three 4-bar phrases, the first repeated), key of C major, quarter=92. The left-hand bass root per bar (I-V-IV-I harmonisation) is our own simple setting; the published original has no piano accompaniment of its own.

meta.subtitle: Traditional French melody, simple two-hand setting in 4/4
meta.trains: A very well-known stepwise-and-small-leap melody in quarter and half notes, over a single sustained bass note per bar - an easy first tune for reading two staves together.

meta.title: Innocence (25 Etudes faciles, Op. 100, No. 5 - opening strain, arranged)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Burgmuller, 25 Etudes faciles et progressives, Op. 100, No. 5 "Innocence" (public domain, published 1852). Measures 1-11 (both hands, right-hand 16th-note and 8th-note pitches and rhythm, left-hand dotted-half triads) were checked note-by-note against the Mutopia Project's public-domain LilyPond edition (piece-info id 214, 25EF-05, typeset by Bas Wassink, key F major, Moderato).
provenance.note: This is our own re-engraving, not a copy of the Mutopia file, and it is an arrangement of the opening strain only (11 of the source's measures): the source's own second strain closes with a more virtuosic ottava-displaced descending/ascending run and a forte chord that we judged too advanced for this shelf slot, so measures 12-16 here are our own closing - a restatement of the opening's 16th-note turn figure (same as measures 1, matching the source's own written repeat structure) followed by a simple three-chord plagal-flavoured cadence, built from the piece's own motifs rather than transcribed from the source's actual ending.

meta.subtitle: Unschuld - opening strain, our own closing
meta.trains: A graceful right-hand melody mixing 16th-note turns with dotted-quarter/eighth figures over a sustained left-hand triad in each bar, in 3/4 at a moderate tempo - light articulation and phrase shading more than raw technique.

meta.title: Für Elise (theme, arranged for this app)

provenance.author: Musicanyya practice material
provenance.basedOn: Beethoven, Für Elise, WoO 59 (public domain, composed c. 1810). A-section pitches and rhythm were checked against the Mutopia Project's public-domain LilyPond engraving (piece-info id 931, fur_Elise_WoO59.ly, typeset by Stelios Samelis) before this simplified transcription.
provenance.note: Theme only: the pickup and bars 1-8 of WoO 59, through the theme's first cadence on the A-minor tonic. The B and C sections of the complete piece are not included, and the ending is simplified to a single-pass cadence instead of the repeat back to bar 1.

meta.subtitle: A-section theme only, simplified arrangement
meta.trains: Melodic phrasing over a broken-chord left-hand accompaniment, with a chromatic passing-tone motif.
departures: Theme only: the pickup and bars 1-8 of WoO 59; the rest of the piece is left out.
Bar 8 ends the piece: the final A is held as a dotted quarter to fill the bar, instead of the first ending's quarter note and the repeat back to the start.
